Evidence about a forest-wide exchange system and its limits
The way trees warn one another of insect attacks
Methods for growing seedlings in deep shade

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?

Why people preferred sun time to railroad time
How faster travel led to a shared way of keeping time
How engineers built more accurate clocks
vocab.answer: How faster travel led to a shared way of keeping time

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?

The history of the building materials used in large cities
The causes and effects of extra warmth in urban areas, and possible solutions
Differences in summer weather between countries

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?

How mother cats take care of their kittens
Why cats are happier than other pets
The different reasons a cat might make a certain sound

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?

How scientists measure how deep the sea is
Why most sea plants live in shallow water close to the shore
How the amount of light changes with depth in the ocean

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why European farmers stopped growing wheat and rye
A new way of farming that made fields more productive
How horses gradually replaced oxen on farms across Europe
Why fallow fields produced the largest harvests
vocab.answer: A new way of farming that made fields more productive

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?

How professional workers can turn their acquaintances into close friends
Why strong ties always outperform weak ties during a job search
The research methods that sociologists use to measure friendship
vocab.answer: A finding about the value of distant contacts and later limits on it
vocab.explain: Main idea (paraphrase): the weak-ties finding, its explanation and the later qualifications. C contradicts the study; B invents a topic the passage never discusses.

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How and why crickets make their sound
Why crickets are found mainly in fields and gardens
How female crickets choose which male to follow
Why crickets are quieter on warm summer nights
vocab.answer: How and why crickets make their sound
vocab.explain: Main idea: the passage explains how the sound is made and what it is used for. D contradicts the text, because crickets chirp faster when it is warm. C is never discussed.

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why silver was more valuable than other metals in ancient trade
How Greek cities competed with Lydia for control of markets
How an official mark on metal made buying and selling simpler
Why ancient governments found it difficult to collect taxes
vocab.answer: How an official mark on metal made buying and selling simpler
vocab.explain: Main idea (paraphrase): stamped pieces of a standard weight removed the need to weigh and test metal. B invents a rivalry that the passage never mentions. D reverses the point; coins made taxes easier to collect.

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why infants prefer attractive toys to the ordinary objects around them
How a different method changed views of what babies understand
Why critics reject every study that measures how long infants look
How infants gradually learn to coordinate their reaching and looking
vocab.answer: How a different method changed views of what babies understand
vocab.explain: Main idea (paraphrase): looking-time studies suggested that infants know more than search tasks had shown. C is too extreme; critics raise a doubt, but they do not reject every study. D turns a detail from the last sentence into the topic.

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why bees and butterflies stop working at night
How some flowers are suited to animals that visit at night
Why moths are more useful to plants than bats are
How gardeners can grow flowers that bloom only in the moonlight
vocab.answer: How some flowers are suited to animals that visit at night
vocab.explain: Main idea (paraphrase): the passage describes how night flowers match moths and bats. A misreads the first sentence; C and D are never discussed.

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?

How a machine for copying text made written words more alike
Why eighteenth-century dictionaries contained many spelling mistakes
How printers set metal type to produce identical pages quickly
vocab.answer: How a machine for copying text made written words more alike

vocab.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?

The methods firms use to recruit and train new employees cheaply
The ways in which economic theory predicts the length of recessions
The advantages of lowering wages instead of dismissing workers

vocab.prompt: What is the main purpose of the notice?

To sell new bicycles to students at a special discount
To recruit volunteer mechanics for the Student Center
To explain new parking rules for bicycles on campus

vocab.prompt: Why was the hike moved?

The bus company cancelled the Sunday trip.
Dangerous conditions are expected in the area.
Not enough members had signed up for the Sunday hike.

vocab.prompt: What is the main change described in the notice?

How long people keep items will depend on whether others want them
The library will begin charging higher fines for all late returns of books
Laptops may now be borrowed for longer periods

vocab.prompt: Where should a student go to look for a lost wallet?

The library front desk
The Student Center café
Campus Security

Overnight parking in two lots will be reserved for residents
Lot E will now close to all vehicles at 10 p.m.
Resident permits will be given out free of charge

Wait until the pool is cleaned

To announce that the print center will close in March
To remind students to renew their ID cards
To advertise a sale on color printers

vocab.prompt: Why did Daniel write the email?

To invite residents to try the new washing machines
To warn neighbors about a planned interruption in service
To complain about the noise from the construction work next door

vocab.explain: Purpose (paraphrase): the water will be turned off for repairs. A misreads who is asking for the repair; B picks a minor detail.

vocab.prompt: What is the main change described in the notice?

Tuition refunds will now cover the first ten weeks of a term
A "W" on the transcript will now lower the grade point average
The period for leaving a class has been extended

vocab.prompt: How can students join a class?
options: By paying for it at the desk
By calling the yoga teacher
By signing up at the front desk
By sending an email to the sports center

vocab.prompt: What is the main purpose of the notice?
options: To announce that the graduation ceremony will be held in the ballroom
To explain how final-year students can get their official photos
To ask graduating students to return the gowns they borrowed
To advertise a photography course for students in their last year

vocab.prompt: Why did Lena write the email?

To ask students to write their names on the paper sign-up sheet
To describe a new procedure for reserving equipment
To remind students that their lab reports are due next week

vocab.prompt: When can students get a new card?
options: Any day of the week, all day
On Saturday and Sunday mornings
From Monday to Friday
Every evening after 4 p.m.

vocab.prompt: Why did Professor Brandt send the email?
options: To remind students about arrangements for Friday's museum trip
To ask students to pay for their museum tickets in advance
To remind students that their response papers are due Monday
To explain why backpacks are not allowed inside the museum galleries

vocab.prompt: What is the main purpose of the notice?
options: To announce that the blue bins on each floor will be removed
To explain where residents should now put certain kinds of waste
To invite residents to help sort the recycling in the basement
To tell residents how they can sign up for a free movie night

vocab.explain: Main purpose (paraphrase): the notice tells residents which bin to use for glass, for recyclables and for items with food on them. A is wrong because the blue bins stay; they simply accept fewer items. D turns a minor detail (the prize drawing) into the purpose.

vocab.prompt: What is the main change described in the notice?
options: The ceramics and printmaking studios will close to everyone at 6 p.m.
Students will need a new kind of ID card to enter the studios by day
Studio staff will now stay until 10 p.m. to help students with the kilns
Night-time access to two studios will depend on prior instruction

vocab.prompt: What do students need to take a bike?

Their student ID card
A one-dollar coin
A form from the office

vocab.prompt: What is the main purpose of the notice?
options: To explain how and when students should ask for special exam arrangements
To announce that the Accessibility Services office is moving to a new building
To tell instructors how to prepare separate rooms for their final exams
To invite students to register with Accessibility Services before midterms
vocab.answer: To explain how and when students should ask for special exam arrangements
vocab.explain: Main purpose (paraphrase): the notice sets out the procedure and the deadline for accommodation requests. C reverses the audience: instructors are only notified. D is a precondition, not the purpose.

vocab.prompt: Why did the office write to Daniel?
options: To confirm that his request to pay in parts was accepted
To remind him that his first payment is already overdue
To explain why his application for a payment plan was refused
To ask him to choose how many payments he would like to make
vocab.answer: To confirm that his request to pay in parts was accepted
vocab.explain: Purpose (paraphrase): "Your plan has been approved." B is not stated: no payment is late yet. C reverses the decision; D is wrong because the office has already set four payments.

vocab.prompt: What is the notice mainly about?
options: A new procedure for getting a place to work with classmates
New opening hours for the library during exam weeks
A plan to add more group study rooms to the library
Rules about the noise level allowed in the group study rooms
vocab.answer: A new procedure for getting a place to work with classmates
vocab.explain: Main idea (paraphrase): rooms are now reserved in the app instead of on paper sheets. B, C and D bring in topics the notice never mentions (hours, new rooms, noise).

vocab.prompt: According to the passage, what did European naturalists believe about fossils before Cuvier's work?
options: They were remnants of once-living organisms.
They were unusual stones produced by geological processes.
They proved the existence of extinct species.
They were the result of comparative anatomy studies.
vocab.answer: They were unusual stones produced by geological processes.
vocab.explain: The passage states that 'European naturalists assumed that fossils were simply unusual stones, products of geological processes rather than remnants of once-living organisms.' That's option B verbatim. Option A is the OPPOSITE — what Cuvier later proved. C and D are anachronistic — those came from Cuvier's work, not before.

vocab.prompt: The word 'expelled' in the passage is closest in meaning to:
options: absorbed
ignored
ejected
weakened
vocab.answer: ejected
vocab.explain: In context, 'algae living within coral tissues are EXPELLED' means they are forced out. 'Ejected' (option C) is the closest synonym. 'Absorbed' is the opposite. 'Ignored' doesn't fit a physical process. 'Weakened' describes a different relationship.

vocab.prompt: What can be inferred from the passage about residential solar adoption in the United States?
options: It has matched the dramatic decline in panel prices.
It is primarily limited by the cost of photovoltaic panels.
It is shaped by factors beyond the cost of panels alone.
It will accelerate automatically as panel prices continue to fall.
vocab.answer: It is shaped by factors beyond the cost of panels alone.
vocab.explain: The passage notes panel prices fell 80% but adoption is 'uneven' AND installation costs now exceed panel costs AND permitting reform could matter as much as further price cuts. The inference: adoption depends on more than panel prices. Option C captures this. A contradicts 'uneven'. B is what was true before the price drop, not now. D is the opposite of the passage's argument.

vocab.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following is NOT a characteristic of Stage 2 sleep?
options: It accounts for about half of total sleep time.
It involves reduced muscle activity.
It is characterized by slower brain waves.
It is the deepest stage of sleep.
vocab.answer: It is the deepest stage of sleep.
vocab.explain: The passage attributes 'deepest sleep stages' to Stages 3 and 4 (slow-wave sleep), NOT Stage 2. Options A, B, C are all directly stated about Stage 2. Option D is wrong — that belongs to Stages 3-4.

vocab.prompt: Why does the author mention the British suffragettes' window-smashing and chaining tactics?
options: To criticize violent political activism.
To show that radical tactics alienated the public.
To illustrate the range of methods suffrage movements used.
To argue that peaceful petitions were ineffective.
vocab.answer: To illustrate the range of methods suffrage movements used.
vocab.explain: The British example follows the sentence 'a range of tactics—peaceful petitions, mass demonstrations, hunger strikes, even property destruction.' It serves as a CONCRETE ILLUSTRATION of that range. Option C captures the rhetorical purpose. A and D project a stance the author doesn't take; B describes one consequence but not the author's PURPOSE for including the example.

Wait outside until staff say they can return
Stay in their rooms for about fifteen minutes
Meet in the lobby of Hall B

Dr. Morales asked for a larger screen.
Too many people signed up for the usual room.
The start time of the lecture changed.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker recommend?

Bringing a participation form
Sitting in the assigned section
Arriving before the talk begins

questions.prompt: What will happen on Saturday?

The gym will be closed.
The gym will open at eight.
A swimming class will start.

It will close on Sunday.
It will open at eight a.m.
It will be cleaned this week.

They will arrive ten minutes later than usual.

questions.prompt: Why will the library stay open late?

Because it is being cleaned
Because students have exams
Because new books arrived

questions.explain: Reason.

At the front desk
By calling the library
On the library website

To invite residents to a cooking event

New students on campus
Staff at the activities desk
Teachers of evening classes

They will not be accepted

A change to the date of the first lab session
Problems that students have had with access cards
How the safety quiz will count toward the final grade

Fewer drivers work in the afternoon
Many students are traveling to class then
The old timetable caused long delays at most stops

It will leave later than it does now
It will run every twenty minutes
It will no longer stop at the library

To invite students to learn about studying overseas
To remind students that applications are due
To report a change to Wednesday's lectures

Spaces at some universities are taken quickly

Baker Hall will be closed on Thursday
The professor wants students to sit farther apart
The start time of the exam has been moved

They should go to the Baker Hall auditorium
They may need to leave earlier than usual

In summer, leaves are green because they contain a large amount of chlorophyll, a substance that helps plants make food from sunlight. Leaves also contain yellow and orange substances, but the strong green color usually hides them.
In autumn, days become shorter and cooler. Trees stop producing chlorophyll, and the green color slowly fades. The yellow and orange colors that were there all along become visible. reading.title: Color Words and Perception
reading.passage:
Languages differ considerably in how they divide the color spectrum. Russian, for instance, obligatorily distinguishes between lighter blues (goluboy) and darker blues (siniy), whereas English speakers use a single basic term. This raises a question that has long intrigued linguists and psychologists: does the vocabulary a person habitually uses shape the way that person actually perceives the world?
Experimental evidence suggests a modest but measurable influence. In one study, Russian speakers distinguished between two shades of blue more rapidly when the shades straddled the boundary between goluboy and siniy than when both fell within a single category; English speakers showed no comparable advantage. Crucially, the effect vanished when participants simultaneously performed a verbal task that occupied their linguistic resources.
Researchers therefore caution against strong claims. Language does not appear to determine what people are capable of seeing; it seems instead to provide a convenient shortcut that accelerates certain judgments whenever linguistic processing is available.

To explain why English speakers performed poorly overall

reading.title: Underground Fungal Networks
reading.passage:
Beneath most forests lies an extensive web of fungal threads known as mycorrhizal networks. These fungi colonize the roots of trees, supplying them with water and mineral nutrients such as phosphorus in exchange for sugars that the trees produce through photosynthesis.
Because a single network can connect the roots of many different trees, researchers have proposed that carbon and other resources may travel from one tree to another through these shared connections. Some experiments have reported that seedlings growing in deep shade receive carbon from larger neighbors, which might improve their chances of survival.
Nevertheless, the more dramatic claims, for instance that mature trees deliberately nurture their offspring or warn neighbors of insect attacks, remain contested. Critics note that many field studies were small, that the direction of transfer is difficult to measure, and that fungi may move resources primarily for their own benefit rather than for that of the forest.

questions.answer: To give an example of evidence that resources may move between trees

reading.title: The Invention of Standard Time
reading.passage:
Until the late nineteenth century, most towns set their clocks by the sun. Noon was the moment when the sun stood highest in the sky, so the time in one city could differ by several minutes from the time in a city a short distance to the east or west.
This local system caused few problems while travel was slow. The arrival of railroads, however, changed the situation. Each railway company kept its own schedule, and a single station might display several clocks showing different times. Passengers often missed connections.
In 1883, railroads in the United States and Canada adopted a system of time zones, each differing from its neighbor by exactly one hour. Many communities at first resisted giving up "sun time," but the convenience of the new system gradually won acceptance.

reading.title: Urban Heat Islands
reading.passage:
On a summer afternoon, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. Scientists call this an urban heat island. The main cause is the material that cities are built from: asphalt, concrete and brick absorb sunlight during the day and slowly release that heat at night.
Cities also lack the natural cooling that plants provide. Trees shade the ground, and they release water vapor through their leaves, which cools the surrounding air in much the same way that sweat cools skin. Where green spaces are replaced by roads and buildings, this effect disappears.
The consequences go beyond discomfort. Warmer nights prevent people from recovering from daytime heat, and heat waves in cities are linked to more hospital visits. Some cities now paint roofs white, plant trees along streets and build parks, and early results suggest that these simple changes can lower local temperatures noticeably.

Below that is the twilight zone. Only a little blue light reaches it, and plants cannot grow there. Deeper still, below 1,000 meters, the water is completely dark. Many animals in this deep zone make their own light. They use it to find food, to attract partners, or to confuse enemies.

reading.title: The Three-Field System
reading.passage:
For many centuries, farmers across much of Europe divided their land into two large fields. Each year, one field was planted with grain, while the other was deliberately left unplanted, or fallow, so that the soil could recover its natural fertility. This method protected the soil, but it meant that half of the available land produced nothing in any given year.
Around the eighth century, many villages began organizing their land into three fields instead. One field was sown with wheat or rye in the autumn, a second was planted in spring with oats, peas, or beans, and the third was allowed to rest. The crops then rotated to a different field each year.
This change brought two significant advantages. First, two-thirds of the land was now under cultivation at any time. Second, peas and beans naturally return nitrogen to the soil, so the fields remained productive for longer. The additional oats also supported more horses, which could plow considerably faster than oxen.

options: measure

questions.explain: Vocabulary in context: the field rested so that the soil could "recover" (regain) its natural fertility. B borrows "protected" from the next sentence.

options: Oats were planted in autumn instead of spring

reading.title: The Strength of Weak Ties
reading.passage:
Sociologists distinguish between strong ties, such as those connecting close friends and relatives, and weak ties, which link acquaintances who interact only occasionally. Intuitively, one might assume that strong ties constitute the more valuable resource, since close contacts are typically more willing to offer assistance.
A frequently cited study of professional workers, however, found that people who had obtained jobs through personal contacts more often heard about the position from acquaintances than from close friends. The explanation proposed was structural: members of a tightly knit circle tend to know the same people and encounter the same information, whereas acquaintances move in different social circles and can therefore transmit news that would otherwise remain inaccessible.
Subsequent research has qualified this conclusion. Strong ties appear more influential when information is scarce or when a recommendation requires considerable trust, and the advantage of weak ties seems to depend on the type of labor market. Nevertheless, the central insight, that the value of a connection lies partly in the novelty of what it can provide, has proved remarkably durable.

options: A finding about the value of distant contacts and later limits on it

questions.answer: A finding about the value of distant contacts and later limits on it
questions.explain: Main idea (paraphrase): the weak-ties finding, its explanation and the later qualifications. C contradicts the study; B invents a topic the passage never discusses.

questions.answer: limited
questions.explain: Vocabulary in context: later research "qualified" the conclusion, i.e. limited it by adding conditions. A is another meaning of "qualified" that does not fit here; C is too strong, because the central insight survived.

To describe how acquaintances eventually become close friends

On summer evenings, the sound of crickets fills many fields and gardens. Only male crickets make this sound. A male rubs the edge of one wing against a row of small ridges on the other wing, a little like running a fingernail along a comb.
Most chirping is meant to attract females, which hear the sound through tiny openings on their front legs. Males also use a different song to warn other males to stay away. Crickets chirp faster when the air is warm and more slowly when it is cool, so some people use them to estimate the temperature.

reading.title: The First Coins
reading.passage:
For thousands of years, people traded using pieces of metal, such as silver, whose value depended on their weight and purity. Every sale therefore required a scale, and buyers often cut bits from a larger piece to pay the exact amount. Sellers also had to worry that the metal had been mixed with cheaper materials.
More than 2,600 years ago, rulers in Lydia, a kingdom in what is now western Turkey, began producing small lumps of metal of a standard weight and stamping each one with an official image. The stamp acted as a guarantee: people no longer needed to weigh or test every piece, because the state stood behind its value.
The idea spread quickly to Greek cities, which created their own designs. Before long, coins were used not only in markets but also to pay soldiers and collect taxes, which made it far easier for governments to manage large economies.

options: Why silver was more valuable than other metals in ancient trade

How an official mark on metal made buying and selling simpler
Why ancient governments found it difficult to collect taxes
questions.answer: How an official mark on metal made buying and selling simpler
questions.explain: Main idea (paraphrase): stamped pieces of a standard weight removed the need to weigh and test metal. B invents a rivalry that the passage never mentions. D reverses the point; coins made taxes easier to collect.

options: an assurance
a decoration
a payment

questions.explain: Vocabulary in context: the stamp was a guarantee because the state "stood behind" the value of each piece, so it was an assurance. B describes what the image looks like, not what it does.

To explain how merchants made their own coins
To suggest that buyers often tried to cheat sellers
To illustrate how awkward payment was before coins

reading.title: What Infants Expect
reading.passage:
For much of the twentieth century, the dominant account of infant cognition held that babies younger than about eight months lack object permanence, the understanding that objects continue to exist when they are out of sight. This conclusion rested largely on search tasks: when an attractive toy was covered by a cloth, young infants typically made no attempt to retrieve it.
Beginning in the 1980s, however, researchers adopted an alternative method that did not depend on reaching. Exploiting infants' tendency to look longer at surprising events, they presented apparently impossible scenes, such as a screen rotating straight through the space occupied by a hidden box. Infants as young as four months stared reliably longer at these outcomes, suggesting that they mentally represented the concealed object.
Critics caution that prolonged looking may reflect perceptual novelty rather than genuine reasoning about objects. Even so, the findings have persuaded many developmental psychologists that earlier failures revealed limitations in planning and coordinating actions rather than an absence of knowledge.

questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why infants prefer attractive toys to the ordinary objects around them
How a different method changed views of what babies understand
Why critics reject every study that measures how long infants look
How infants gradually learn to coordinate their reaching and looking
questions.answer: How a different method changed views of what babies understand
questions.explain: Main idea (paraphrase): looking-time studies suggested that infants know more than search tasks had shown. C is too extreme; critics raise a doubt, but they do not reject every study. D turns a detail from the last sentence into the topic.

questions.prompt: The word "Exploiting" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: Paying no attention to
Measuring precisely
Calling into question
Making use of
questions.answer: Making use of
questions.explain: Vocabulary in context: researchers exploited, that is, made use of, infants' habit of looking longer at surprising events. B is tempting because looking time was measured, but the verb refers to taking advantage of the habit.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention "a screen rotating straight through the space occupied by a hidden box"?
options: To illustrate an event that should surprise an infant aware of the box
To show how researchers taught infants to reach for objects behind screens
To describe a toy that infants found more attractive than a cloth
To explain why earlier search tasks produced unreliable results
questions.answer: To illustrate an event that should surprise an infant aware of the box
questions.explain: Author's purpose: the impossible scene is an example of an event that only surprises an infant who represents the hidden box. B is wrong because the new method "did not depend on reaching". D is not the reason the example is given.

They were probably reacting to the novelty of the cloth
questions.answer: They may have known it was there but been unable to act on it
questions.explain: Inference: the last sentence says earlier failures reflected limits in "planning and coordinating actions" rather than missing knowledge. D applies the critics' novelty argument to the wrong studies. B is never claimed in the passage.

questions.answer: Infants might look longer simply because a scene is new to them
questions.explain: Detail (paraphrase): longer looking "may reflect perceptual novelty", meaning the scene is simply new to the infant. A sounds like a typical criticism, but the passage never mentions how many infants were tested.

reading.title: How Printing Changed Spelling
reading.passage:
Before the printing press reached England in the late fifteenth century, English spelling varied widely. Writers spelled words as they heard them, and the same scribe might write a common word in two or three ways on a single page.
Printing gradually reduced this variety. Because a printer produced hundreds of identical copies, readers across the country began to see the same forms again and again. Printers also had practical reasons to settle on fixed spellings, since consistent forms made it faster to set the metal type for each page.
The change was slow, however. Early printers sometimes added or removed letters simply to fill a line evenly, and many spellings did not become stable until dictionaries appeared in the eighteenth century. Even so, historians generally agree that printing started the movement toward standard spelling.

reading.title: Why Wages Rarely Fall
reading.passage:
Elementary economic theory predicts that when the demand for labor declines, wages should fall until employers are again willing to hire everyone seeking work. Empirical studies, however, consistently find that nominal wages are remarkably resistant to reduction, even during severe recessions; firms typically respond to weaker demand by dismissing employees rather than by lowering pay.
Economists have proposed several explanations for this rigidity. Surveys of managers indicate that wage cuts are perceived as unfair and consequently damage morale, diminishing the effort of the very employees a firm most wishes to retain. Efficiency-wage theory extends this reasoning, arguing that paying above the market rate can be profitable because it reduces turnover and the considerable costs of recruiting and training replacements.
Wage rigidity has significant consequences. Because pay does not adjust, the burden of a downturn is concentrated on those who lose their jobs rather than distributed across the entire workforce, which may help explain why unemployment rises so sharply during recessions.

questions.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The reasons wages seldom fall and what this means during downturns
The methods firms use to recruit and train new employees cheaply
The ways in which economic theory predicts the length of recessions
The advantages of lowering wages instead of dismissing workers
questions.answer: The reasons wages seldom fall and what this means during downturns
questions.explain: Main idea (paraphrase): the passage explains why wages are rigid and how this concentrates the cost of recessions. D reverses the evidence; B is a minor detail inside one explanation.

questions.prompt: The word "rigidity" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: unfair treatment
unwillingness to change
a period of rapid growth

questions.answer: unwillingness to change
questions.explain: Vocabulary in context: "this rigidity" refers back to wages being "resistant to reduction", that is, not changing. A is the reason given by managers, not the meaning of the word.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention surveys of managers?
options: To show that managers misunderstand basic economic theory
To prove that recessions are caused by unfair treatment of employees
To support the claim that cutting pay can lower workers' effort
To compare how often firms dismiss workers in different countries
questions.answer: To support the claim that cutting pay can lower workers' effort
questions.explain: Author's purpose: the surveys support the idea that wage cuts "damage morale, diminishing the effort" of employees. B overstates the claim into a cause of recessions; A and D are not in the passage.

Training new employees costs less than keeping experienced ones

questions.answer: Generous salaries can end up saving a company money
questions.explain: Inference: paying above the market rate "can be profitable" because it lowers turnover costs. B overstates "reduces turnover" as "rarely need to hire"; C reverses the costs; D contradicts the theory.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what is one effect of wage rigidity?
options: All employees share equally in the losses of a recession

questions.answer: The costs of a downturn fall mainly on workers who are dismissed

Professor: When governments fund research, they typically focus on either basic science (research without immediate practical application) or applied science (research aimed at solving specific problems). Given limited budgets, which should governments prioritize? Why?
